hero.headline: Code Gates Catch What Judges Miss
hero.dek: Week 2 builds added checks between the first draft and the send. The strongest ones let code, not the model, decide what is risky.
hero.intro: Most builds this week put a check between the model's first answer and the action that follows. Drew Patel's support desk showed why: a judge scored a risky reply 9 out of 10, and a code flag stopped it. Blake Torres moved date checks out of the prompt and into code, and Avery Quinn tested the failure path on purpose.

spotlights.title: Support Reply Desk
spotlights.author: Drew Patel
spotlights.summary: A writer drafts support replies from the policy, a judge scores them, code flags risky tickets, and a person approves every reply in Telegram.
spotlights.narrative: Drew's desk layers three checks. Code sets the risk flag for refunds over $100, so risk never depends on the model. The judge scores tone and accuracy, and a person approves the final reply.
spotlights.testResult: In one test the judge gave 9 out of 10 to a reply that promised a refund over the limit; the code flag stopped it.
spotlights.fromTheThread: Blake asked whether the judge sees the risk flag. Drew said not yet; he wants to see whether it notices on its own first.
spotlights.worthBorrowing: Let code flag high-risk items, and keep a person on the final call even when the score passes.

spotlights.title: Recipe Scaler with a Judge
spotlights.author: Avery Quinn
spotlights.summary: Scales a recipe to a new serving size; a judge scores each draft out of 10 and 8 passes.
spotlights.narrative: Below 8, one revision runs with the judge's notes, at most twice, then the draft goes to Avery. A code node now rejects any ingredient without a unit.
spotlights.testResult: Avery raised the threshold to 10 for one run to watch the revision path work.
spotlights.fromTheThread: Blake suggested a hard check on units; Avery added one in code.
spotlights.worthBorrowing: Test the failure path with real outputs by raising the threshold for one run.

spotlights.title: Expense Logger with Code Checks
spotlights.author: Blake Torres
spotlights.summary: Extracts amount, date and category from emailed receipts and checks them in code before logging.
spotlights.narrative: Failed checks retry up to three times. After that, the receipt lands in a review sheet with the reason.
spotlights.testResult: The checks caught a $75 grocery receipt the model had dated last year.
spotlights.fromTheThread: Drew asked what happens after the third retry; Blake explained the review sheet.
spotlights.worthBorrowing: Check dates and amounts in code, not in the prompt.

failurePath.title: Support Reply Desk
failurePath.author: Drew Patel
failurePath.whatFailed: The judge scored a reply 9 out of 10 even though it promised a refund over the $100 limit.
failurePath.whatCaughtIt: A code rule that flags refunds over $100 routed the reply to a person.
failurePath.lesson: A high judge score is not proof. Put hard rules in code.

synthesis.text: Classmates kept asking what happens after the last retry, which pushed authors to describe their fallback paths.
Several replies pointed to checks that belong in code rather than in a judge's prompt.

takeaways.title: A high score isn't proof
takeaways.text: A judge passed a reply that broke policy. Hard rules belong in code or with a person.

takeaways.title: Cap the loop, then hand off
takeaways.text: Give every retry loop a maximum and a place to go when it runs out.

takeaways.title: Test the failure path on purpose
takeaways.text: Raise the threshold or feed a known-bad input to see what your safeguards catch.
